research_notes:
I found and checked 13 sources for the one sec alternative article. There's one finding the writer has to work around: one sec can already interrupt you mid-session, according to its own FAQ, so the article can't say a mid-scroll pause is something one sec lacks. The research notes are below. All facts were checked on 2026-11-17.

---

# Research notes: "one sec alternative"

## SERP ANALYSIS

**Who ranks:** The results are almost all sites run by app makers, plus one aggregator.
- **AlternativeTo** (alternativeto.net/software/one-sec/) ranks first and has many paginated variants. It is a crowd-sourced list: Mindful, LeechBlock, Cold Turkey, Mindful Guard, Reef, QuestPhone, ClearSpace and others. It doesn't say how the list is ordered (the "likes" counts don't match the order), it puts a paid ad (FocusMe) in slot 5, and it has no description of one sec.
- **habitdoom.com:** a listicle with a "short version," a summary table, one review per app, a "how to pick" section and an FAQ. The order is ScreenZen, Habit Doom, Opal, Apple Screen Time, Brick. It is written to make its own app the "closest match." It only says who owns the site in the footer, cites no research (one Reddit thread), and contradicts itself on ScreenZen's pricing. It does say the 10-second pause "stops working," but it never talks about interrupting a scroll that's already underway.
- **getdull.app:** Dull's own site. Its list is Dull ("Best content filter") first, then UNDOOMED and Opal. It mentions the Max Planck 57% figure twice with no link. Its angle is that one sec changes how often you open an app but not what you see once you're inside. Ownership is disclosed only in the footer.
- **TaskGate's site** (vercel): its own app is ranked #1 as "Recommended," followed by ScreenZen, Opal, Forest and unhookd. There's no disclosure. Several prices look attached to the wrong apps (for example "$4.99/month" under ScreenZen, and Opal's yearly price showing up in the ScreenZen row). It claims one sec costs "$50/year" with no source, says one sec has "research-backed credibility" without citing anything, and has no FAQ.
- Also in the results: Product Hunt, openalternative.co, and vendor posts from repscroll and dev.to.

**What they do well:** Summary tables, "best for" labels, and splitting apps into a soft pause/friction group and a hard-block group (Opal, Brick).

**What they get wrong or leave out:**
- Every brand-run page ranks its own app first, and none discloses that in the body.
- They cite almost no research. Nobody links the PNAS paper or reports its caveats (no control group, a co-author created one sec). Nobody mentions the CHI 2024 finding that usage rebounds.
- Prices are unchecked or wrong, with no check date.
- None of them covers the scroll that has already wound you up. They all treat the problem as the moment of opening the app. None mentions that the feed itself can leave you wired, or offers anything for regulating once you're in it.
- Google Pause Point is barely covered. Pages written for iPhone users skip that it's Android-only.

**Format to match:** A comparison roundup with a short answer first, a summary table, one section per app with the same fields, "which to pick" lines, and an FAQ. Titles in these results add the year ("2026"), but our playbook says no year in the title.

## GAPS AND ANGLE

1. **Honesty about one sec itself.** Its FAQ says interventions can appear on opening, "after a delay (X minutes in)," or "repeat after a set time." That means one sec already offers some mid-session nudges. ScreenZen's listing also has "Interrupt your scrolling: Check your distracting apps for short periods of time so you don't get sucked in." **The writer must not claim that only DeRot interrupts a session.** The honest difference for DeRot is the purpose: a pause timed for when the feed has wound you up, built around bringing you back down (calm breathing as the main event), not about deciding whether to open the app or making you jump through a hoop to earn access.
2. **What the evidence says about tapping through.** In the PNAS field study, the share of opening attempts people dismissed fell from 43% in week 1 to about 32–34% from week 3 on. Habituation shows up in the data, and readers' "I tap straight through it now" feeling has research behind it. The CHI 2024 study found that users who took breaks from the friction "quickly rebounded" when they came back. Nobody in the SERP uses this.
3. **The most effective part of one sec was the option to back out**, not the message and not the wait on its own (PNAS online experiment, N=500). This is useful and new for readers: what makes a friction app work is a clear exit, not the length of the delay.
4. **Neutral, disclosed structure.** Disclose in the first 100 words that DeRot makes an app in this category, and rank no DeRot at all. No current result does this.
5. **Pause Point, clarified for iPhone users.** Google's help page lists only "Pixel 11 series running Android 17 and later." It isn't on iPhone. (Trade press reports a rollout to older Pixels and a OnePlus beta, but that is not confirmed by Google, so treat it as reported.)
6. **Grouping by what each app does instead:** friction/delay (ScreenZen, ClearSpace, Pause Point), hard blockers (Opal Deep Focus, Brick, Apple Screen Time), and breathing/regulation (where DeRot sits, unranked).
7. **Call out Brick or Opal Deep Focus as the better pick** for anyone who wants a real lockout. Brick says there is "no quick override."

**Suggested if-then lines:**
- If you want what one sec does, but free → ScreenZen. It's free and supported by optional tips; on iOS it has delays that get longer, open limits, and "Minimal" mode for removing Reels and Shorts.
- If you want a pause plus open limits and accountability on iPhone → ClearSpace.
- If you're on a Pixel → Pause Point is built in.
- If you want a lockout you can't skip → Opal Deep Focus, or Brick (a physical tap to unblock).
- If you want something free and built in with no third-party app → Apple Screen Time (limits and schedules, not a pause).
- If you liked one sec but the problem is how you feel 15 minutes in → check one sec's own "after X minutes" intervention setting first, then see "Where DeRot fits."

## SAFETY

- **Breathing:** If you feel dizzy, lightheaded or tingly, go back to normal breathing. Keep exhales easy, not forced.
- **Breath holds and fast breathing** (box holds, cyclic hyperventilation) aren't for everyone. That includes pregnancy, heart or lung conditions, a history of fainting, or panic. Balban 2023 excluded people with heart disease, glaucoma, seizure history, pregnancy and several psychiatric conditions, and 10% of participants reported negative experiences. Plain slow breathing with longer exhales is the gentlest choice.
- **Claims:** Don't say any app or breathing pattern treats anxiety or "addiction." Say breathing "can help you feel calmer" or "may reduce stress." The Balban study found mood and respiratory-rate effects, but no HRV change and no anxiety advantage over mindfulness.
- **Evidence:** The friction research is promising but limited. There was no control group in the field study, the app's makers are co-authors, much of the data is self-reported, and users rebounded after breaks. Say this plainly.
- **Hard blockers:** Point out emergency access (Brick's "five Emergency Unbricks," and Opal Deep Focus can't be cancelled), so readers keep access to calls and maps.
- **Getting help:** If scrolling is tied to persistent anxiety, sleep problems or low mood, talk to a professional. In a crisis, contact local emergency services or call/text 988 in the US.
